title: Capital is the constraint
lede: Every page so far has measured a trade by its P&L. A desk measures it by P&L per dollar of capital tied up, and the capital is set by a margin rule, not by the premium. This page uses two simplified rules to show how the same trade earns three different returns, and why a position is sized by what its margin becomes in a bad week.

chapters.title: One trade, three capital numbers
chapters.dek: The premium is what you collect. The requirement is what you must post. The return is one divided by the other, and the rule sets the denominator.

figures.title: P&L across the range a risk-based rule scans
figures.caption: The put you buy underneath costs a third of the premium and cuts the capital by more than half. That exchange is the reason spreads exist.

checks.q: Two trades each expect to make $1,000. One ties up $5,000 for a month, the other $20,000 for a month. Capital is your limit. Which do you prefer, all else equal?
checks.right: The first: you can do four of them with the capital the second uses
checks.why: The first. 20% on capital against 5%. The caution is in "all else equal": a small requirement often means a rule that has not seen the risk, and the next chapter is about what happens when it does.

chapters.text: Sell one 30-day 95 put on a $100 stock at 30 vol. The blue line is what the position makes or loses if the stock moves today; the green line is the same put with a 90 put bought underneath it. The red dots mark the worst point in a 15% range, which is what a risk-based rule charges. P&L across the range a risk-based rule scans The scan, cell by cell: the requirement is the worst one The same premium over three denominators The trade The put you buy underneath costs a third of the premium and cuts the capital by more than half. That exchange is the reason spreads exist. The put brings in $132. Under the strategy-based formula it ties up $1,632 , so keeping the whole premium is an 8.1% return on capital for the month. Under the risk-based rule the worst loss in the scan is $872 , and the same $132 is 15.2%. Nothing about the trade changed; the account type did. Buy the 90 put and the credit falls to $93, but the most the position can lose is $407 , and the return on that is 22.7%. The spread earns less money and more per dollar of capital, which is the comparison that matters when capital is what you run out of. A hedged position is the extreme case. A conversion's P&L is flat across the whole scan, so a risk-based rule asks for almost nothing and the binding number becomes a minimum or a haircut on the stock. That is why financing trades are run in size on small spreads, and why their return is quoted on the balance sheet they use and not on premium. Trader's lens A desk rarely asks what a trade makes. It asks what the trade makes per unit of the scarce thing : capital, balance sheet, or a risk limit. Most firms charge each desk for the capital it ties up, so a trade is judged on its return on that charge, and two trades with the same premium can be a good use of the book and a bad one. Read the denominator first. The rule, not the trade, sets it. A spread sells a little premium to buy back a lot of capital. When capital binds, that is usually a good exchange. A requirement that looks small is a rule that has not seen the risk yet. Chapter 02 is what happens when it does. Rule of thumb: quote a short-premium trade as return on capital per month, never as premium. [equation: return on capital = P&L ÷ requirement risk-based requirement = − min over the scan of ( repriced value − today's value )] Reads as: divide what the trade makes by what it ties up; and under a risk-based rule, what it ties up is the largest loss found when the stock is walked across the range. Try this Sell the put at the money instead. Predict which grows faster, the premium or the risk-based requirement.

chapters.title: The requirement moves against you
chapters.dek: A position sized to today's margin is sized to a number that rises exactly as your equity falls.

figures.title: Equity and requirement as the stock moves
figures.caption: The two lines close from both sides. Where they meet, the position is reduced for you, at whatever the market is paying that day.

figures.title: Run the account through a sell-off
figures.caption: You see only the days that have happened. On the first path the stock falls for nine days, gaps 6% on the ninth to $87.68, and recovers to $96.22 by the last day, above the strike. Held without acting, the account using 30% of its capital is never called and ends up $2,943. At 50% the call comes on the gap day and the account ends down $6,168. At 80% the first call comes on day 4, there are six in all, and it ends down $25,365, on a stock that finished above the strike. Buying back a quarter on days 5 and 6 keeps the 50% account out of every call.

checks.q: A short-option book uses 60% of its capital as margin and has just lost 8% of its equity in a selloff. What has most likely happened to its excess?
checks.right: It fell by much more, because the requirement rose while equity fell
checks.why: Much more. Excess is equity minus requirement, and a selloff moves both the wrong way: the loss comes out of equity, and the same move and higher vol put more into the requirement. In the figure a 13% loss of equity removed 46% of the excess.

chapters.text: An account with $100,000 sells the same 95 puts until the risk-based requirement uses half its capital. That is 57 contracts and $7,538 of premium. Now the stock falls, and implied vol rises one point for each 1% it loses. The blue line is the account's equity. The red line is what the rule demands. Equity and requirement as the stock moves Sizing and the market The two lines close from both sides. Where they meet, the position is reduced for you, at whatever the market is paying that day. After a 5% fall the position has lost $13,105, so equity is $86,895. The requirement has not stayed at $49,685; the puts are now at the money and more volatile, and the rule wants $59,792 . Excess has gone from $50,315 to $27,103 on a loss of thirteen thousand. The lines meet at a fall of 10.7% . Utilization is the whole lever. At 80% the account holds 91 contracts and the call comes at a fall of 2.8%, a move this stock makes about one month in three. At 30% it holds 34 and survives to 24.8%. The premium collected rises in a straight line with size; the distance to a forced exit collapses. So the sizing question is not "what does margin allow today" but "what will the requirement be after the move I must be able to survive, and will I still have excess". Work it backwards: pick the stress, reprice the book and the margin there, and size so equity still clears it. Page 16's put-writers who are still in business are the ones who did this, and the rule that leverage is what turns a drawdown into ruin is this figure stated in words. Two things make the real case worse than the figure. Requirements are raised by decision as well as by formula: clearing firms lift house margins in stressed markets, on the names under stress. And everyone with the same position meets the same call on the same day, which is why forced selling shows up as a gap and not as a slide. The curve above assumes the move happens all at once. Real sell-offs take days, time passes, and you get to act along the way, so run one. You start each run short the 95 puts, sized to the share of capital you choose. Each day the stock moves, implied vol rises with the fall, the puts decay, and the rule reprices your requirement. You can buy back a quarter of the position at a ten-cent cost, or hold. If equity falls below the requirement, the broker buys back as many puts as it takes, at thirty-five cents over the middle of the market. Trader's lens A risk manager watches excess , not equity, and asks one question every morning: what is my excess after the worst day I can imagine, with vol up? A book that can answer "still positive" is never forced to sell. A book that cannot will sell at the bottom of the gap, when every seller is a forced one and the market charges for it. The buffer you need is set by the move, not by today's margin. Houses raise requirements in stress, on the names under stress, by decision as well as by formula. Cutting early is cheap insurance; being cut is the most expensive trade you will make. Rule of thumb: size so the requirement after a two-sigma day with vol up still leaves excess. Try this Use 80% of capital. Predict how far the stock can fall before the call. Then run the same sell-off at both sizes. Predict which account is still short the puts when the stock recovers. Derivation — what the two rules are, and what they leave out The strategy-based figure is the standard formula for an uncovered short equity put, applied per contract. [equation: requirement = premium + max( 20% × S − out-of-the-money amount , 10% × K )] Reads as: the premium you received, plus a fifth of the stock price reduced by how far out of the money the put is, with a floor of a tenth of the strike. The risk-based figure reprices the position at ten stock prices from 15% down to 15% up, at unchanged volatility, and takes the largest loss. Where it breaks. Real portfolio margin also offsets correlated underlyings, applies a minimum per contract, adds charges for concentrated or illiquid positions, and treats indexes with a narrower range than single stocks. It does not shock volatility in the standard scan, which is why chapter 02 has to add the vol move by hand. Firms that clear their own trades are bound by net-capital haircuts instead, a third calculation with its own schedule. None of these is a model of what you can lose; each is a rule about what you must post.
